content: Critical illness is often accompanied by uncontrolled inflammation and vascular damage, which can lead to multiple organ failure and death. Antithrombin III (AT III) is an anticoagulant that also possesses anti-inflammatory properties. However, the efficacy and potential adverse effects of AT III supplementation in critically ill patients remain uncertain. This systematic review, originally published in 2008 and updated in 2015, aimed to evaluate the effects of AT III on mortality and its associated benefits and harms in critically ill patients. The primary objective of this review was to assess the impact of AT III on mortality in critically ill patients. Secondary objectives included evaluating the benefits and harms of AT III, including complications related to the intervention, bleeding events, its effects on sepsis and disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), and the length of stay in the intensive care unit (ICU) and hospital. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) regardless of publication status, language, or blinding. A total of 30 RCTs involving 3933 participants were included, with 3882 participants analyzed for the primary outcome of mortality. Data were independently extracted by two authors, and disagreements were resolved through discussion. Risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were calculated for dichotomous outcomes, and subgroup analyses were performed to explore the effects of AT III in different populations and under varying conditions. The pooled analysis of all trials, regardless of bias, showed no statistically significant effect of AT III on mortality (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.03, I² = 0%, fixed-effect model, moderate quality of evidence). Trials with a low risk of bias also demonstrated no significant effect on mortality (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.04, I² = 0%, fixed-effect model). Similarly, trials with a high risk of bias showed no significant effect (RR 0.94, 95% CI 0.77 to 1.14, I² = 0%, fixed-effect model). In participants with severe sepsis and DIC, the effect on mortality remained non-significant (RR 0.95, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.03, I² = 0%, fixed-effect model, moderate quality of evidence). Subgroup and sensitivity analyses, including those based on risk of bias, patient populations (e.g., sepsis, trauma, obstetrics, pediatrics), and the use of concomitant heparin, did not reveal any statistically significant benefits of AT III. Regarding secondary outcomes, the risk of complications specific to the intervention was not significantly increased (RR 1.26, 95% CI 0.83 to 1.92, I² = 0%, random-effects model, very low quality of evidence). For complications unrelated to the intervention, the RR was 0.71 (95% CI 0.08 to 6.11, I² = 28%, random-effects model, very low quality of evidence). Non-bleeding complications also showed no significant difference (RR 0.72, 95% CI 0.42 to 1.25, I² = 0%, fixed-effect model, very low quality of evidence). However, AT III was associated with a statistically significant increase in bleeding events (RR 1.58, 95% CI 1.35 to 1.84, I² = 0%, fixed-effect model, moderate quality of evidence). The mean difference in the amount of red blood cells transfused was 138.49 mL (95% CI -391.35 to 668.34, I² = 84%, random-effects model, very low quality of evidence). In patients with multiple organ failure (MOF), AT III showed a mean difference of -1.24 days in ICU stay (95% CI -2.18 to -0.29, I² = 48%, random-effects model, very low quality of evidence). For patients with Acute Physiology and Chronic Health Evaluation (APACHE) II and III scores, the mean difference was -2.18 (95% CI -4.36 to -0.00, I² = 0%, fixed-effect model, very low quality of evidence). The incidence of respiratory failure was not significantly affected (RR 0.93, 95% CI 0.76 to 1.14, I² = 32%, random-effects model, moderate quality of evidence). AT III had no statistically significant effect on the duration of mechanical ventilation (mean difference 2.20 days, 95% CI -1.21 to 5.60, I² = 0%, fixed-effect model, very low quality of evidence), the length of ICU stay (mean difference 0.24 days, 95% CI -1.34 to 1.83, I² = 0%, fixed-effect model, very low quality of evidence), or the overall length of hospital stay (mean difference 1.10 days, 95% CI -7.16 to 9.36, I² = 74%, random-effects model, very low quality of evidence). In conclusion, there is insufficient evidence to support the use of AT III supplementation in critically ill patients, including those with sepsis and DIC. AT III did not demonstrate a statistically significant effect on mortality but was associated with an increased risk of bleeding events. Subgroup analyses based on intervention duration, follow-up length, patient groups, and the use of adjuvant heparin did not reveal any differences in the intervention's effects. Most of the included trials were at high risk of bias, and the quality of evidence was very low for most outcomes. Therefore, a large, well-designed RCT without adjuvant heparin is needed to evaluate the role of AT III in critically ill patients, particularly those with severe sepsis and DIC.
